instructional_purpose: Builds the full person/number/gender ending paradigm of the perfect (الماضي) for strong triliteral verbs and explains the stem alternation that appears before consonant-initial endings. It also fixes the third-person masculine singular as the citation shape a learner looks up.
concepts_taught: perfect tense as the completed-action form
citation shape of a verb equals the unmarked third masculine singular
strong (non-weak) root class as the stated scope limit
inventory of thirteen inflected slots across person, number and gender
ending set organised into first-, second- and third-person groups
loss of the vowel on the second radical before consonant-initial endings
dual as an inflectional number distinct from plural
absence of any first-person dual slot
subject identifiable from the ending alone, independent pronoun optional
identical ending set applied to an augmented (Form IV) stem

linguistic_propositions.proposition: In the perfect, person, number and gender are carried entirely by word-final endings; no prefix participates.
The unmarked third masculine singular is the base against which the whole perfect paradigm is described and the shape used for lexicon lookup.
The perfect paradigm contains exactly thirteen distinct inflected shapes, because the second-person dual does not distinguish gender.
The second radical carries sukun before every first- and second-person ending, and keeps its vowel in all third-person slots.
That vowel loss occurs because the language avoids three successive short vowels.
Augmented stems inflect with the same ending set; only the stem to which the endings attach differs.
The independent subject pronoun may be omitted because the ending already identifies the subject (pro-drop).
Middle-vowel differences between strong perfect stems have no effect on the ending set.

recognition_criteria: a consonant-initial ending beginning with ت or ن signals a first- or second-person form and co-occurs with a vowelless second radical
a vowelled second radical with a light vowel-initial or ت-initial third-person marker signals a third-person form
long-alif endings mark dual, waw-alif marks masculine plural, a nun ending marks feminine plural
final short vowel alone separates the first singular from the second masculine and second feminine singular
in unvocalised text several slots share one consonantal skeleton and must be resolved by agreement or discourse context
procedures: take the citation shape of a strong verb
strip to the stem used for endings
choose the person/number/gender slot
if the slot is first or second person, remove the vowel from the second radical
attach the ending prescribed for that slot
for augmented stems, repeat the same steps on the augmented stem without changing the ending set
conditions: scope is limited to roots with no weak letter
the sukun alternation is conditioned by the consonant-initial shape of the ending, not by meaning
dual endings apply only when the referent is exactly two
exceptions: no first-person dual exists; the plural covers two or more speakers
second-person dual collapses the gender distinction that the third-person dual keeps
contrasts: third-person slots versus first/second-person slots with respect to the vowel on the second radical
masculine plural ending versus feminine plural ending in the third person
forms with an overt independent pronoun versus the same forms without one

common_mistakes.pattern: treating the first-person singular and second-person masculine singular perfect as interchangeable
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the two slots differ only in the final short vowel on the ending, so dropping vocalisation collapses them
common_mistakes.correction_principle: read the final vowel when the text is vocalised, and otherwise fix the person from agreement and discourse participants

common_mistakes.pattern: applying a dual ending to a subject of three or more
common_mistakes.why_wrong: dual inflection is licensed only for a referent of exactly two
common_mistakes.correction_principle: count the referent first, then choose dual versus plural inflection

common_mistakes.pattern: keeping the vowel on the second radical while attaching a ت-initial ending
common_mistakes.why_wrong: consonant-initial perfect endings require the preceding radical to be vowelless
common_mistakes.correction_principle: apply the stem alternation before attaching any first- or second-person ending

common_mistakes.pattern: interchanging the third masculine plural and third feminine plural endings
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the two are distinct exponents of gender in the same person and number cell
common_mistakes.correction_principle: select the ending from the person-number-gender cell rather than from plurality alone

isolate the ending

state the slot label and check it against the overt or omitted subject

instructional_purpose: Introduces the imperfect (المضارع) of strong verbs as a circumfixal paradigm: a person-marking prefix plus number/gender endings, and adds a first pass at the three moods signalled on the final position.
concepts_taught: imperfect as the non-past form covering ongoing, habitual and future reference
four person-marking prefixes
endings that add number and gender on top of the prefix
full thirteen-slot imperfect paradigm
three moods and their final markers
mood triggers: particles introducing subordination, the negator that forces jussive
unpredictability of the imperfect stem vowel from the perfect stem vowel
syncretism of second masculine singular with third feminine singular

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The imperfect marks person by a prefix and refines number and gender by an ending, unlike the perfect which uses endings only.
One prefix serves both second person generally and third feminine, so prefix alone does not determine the slot.
The default mood is indicative, marked by a final damma.
Certain subordinating particles put the following imperfect in the subjunctive, marked by a final fatha.
The past-negating particle لم puts the imperfect in the jussive, marked by sukun.
Mood can be read off the final vowel of any imperfect form.
The imperfect stem vowel is lexically stored and cannot be derived from the perfect stem vowel.
The imperative belongs with the jussive as one of the jussive contexts.

recognition_criteria: an imperfect form opens with one of four short-vowel prefixes
the prefix narrows the candidate slots, and the ending selects among them
a long-vowel-plus-nun ending marks dual, masculine plural or second feminine singular
a bare nun ending marks feminine plural
identical prefix-plus-ending shapes for two different slots must be separated by the subject or the surrounding clause
a preceding subordinating or negating particle predicts the final marker
procedures: choose the prefix that matches the person
attach it to the imperfect stem carrying the verb's lexically stored middle vowel
add the number/gender ending for the target slot
determine the syntactic environment
set the final marker to indicative, subjunctive or jussive according to that environment
conditions: the mood marker is determined by what governs the clause, not by the verb itself
the middle vowel must be known per lexeme before the form can be produced
exceptions: the feminine plural slots do not participate in the final-vowel alternation the mood section describes
the slots ending in a nun are affected by mood through that nun rather than through a final short vowel, which the lesson does not state
contrasts: perfect marking by ending only versus imperfect marking by prefix plus ending
indicative versus subjunctive versus jussive final markers
the shared shape of second masculine singular and third feminine singular
the several perfect-to-imperfect stem-vowel correspondences shown side by side
misleading_shortcuts: the rule that mood is visible as a final short vowel is stated without the nun-bearing slots being excepted, so a learner or model will misapply it to dual, masculine plural and second feminine singular forms
listing the imperfect as having three moods without noting that some slots are morphologically fixed invites the assumption that every slot inflects for mood
the perfect-to-imperfect vowel correspondence table can be read as predictive although the lesson itself says the vowel must be learned per verb
one exercise grid pairs a feminine column with a first-person row, which produces a cell where gender is not actually expressed
worked_analysis_stages: identify the prefix
identify the ending

instructional_purpose: Introduces the direct object (المفعول به) as the constituent that receives the verb's action and is marked accusative, and sets out how the accusative is realised across noun classes including attached object pronouns.
concepts_taught: direct object as the receiver of the verb's action
accusative as the case assigned to the direct object

object pronouns realised as endings on the verb
transitivity named as the property of verbs that license an object

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A direct object is always accusative.
The accusative exponent varies by noun class, so fatha is the default rather than the definition of the case.
The sound feminine plural takes a kasra exponent in the accusative rather than fatha.
A small closed set of kinship-type nouns takes a long-vowel accusative exponent when annexed.
The canonical order in a verbal sentence is verb, then subject, then object.
An object pronoun attaches directly to the verb and functions as the direct object.
The direct object is identified by asking what the action was done to.
Verbs that take a direct object are transitive; not all verbs do.

recognition_criteria: a post-verbal noun bearing the accusative exponent for its class, where the agent is separately expressed
a pronominal ending on the verb that is not part of the subject-marking inflection
the class of the noun must be checked before the exponent is read, since dual, sound plurals and diptotes do not use fatha
procedures: locate the verb
locate the agent
ask what the action reached
assign accusative to that constituent
select the exponent from the noun-class table
if the object is pronominal, attach it to the verb instead of writing a separate word
conditions: the verb must be one that licenses an object

exceptions: sound feminine plurals do not show fatha in the accusative

the closed kinship-type set takes a long vowel
pronoun objects are not independently case-marked and occupy the accusative position only positionally

instructional_purpose: Separates verbs that license a direct object from those that do not, gives a test for deciding which a verb is, and shows that an augmented pattern can turn a non-licensing verb into a licensing one.
concepts_taught: intransitive and transitive as named verb classes

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A transitive verb licenses a direct object in the accusative; an intransitive verb does not.
Whether a verb takes a direct object can be decided by trying an accusative noun after it.
Intransitive verbs express their complement through a preposition, which puts the following noun in the genitive.
The causative augmented pattern (أَفْعَلَ) commonly makes a non-licensing verb licensing.
Some verbs alternate, taking either a direct object or a prepositional complement with no change of pattern.
A verb described as taking a prepositional complement is nonetheless classified as transitive.
Transitivity is a property of the lexeme as such.

recognition_criteria: an accusative noun following the verb with the agent separately expressed indicates object-licensing
a preposition immediately after the verb, with a genitive noun, indicates a prepositional complement rather than an object
an augmented causative pattern on a normally non-licensing root predicts an object
a verb appearing in both frames signals an alternating lexeme
procedures: take the verb
attempt an accusative noun as its complement
if that fails, look for the preposition the verb selects
if a causative sense is wanted for a non-licensing verb, derive the augmented pattern and then supply an accusative object
conditions: the test presupposes that the intended sense of the verb is fixed first
the transitivising effect of the augmented pattern is described as frequent, not automatic
alternating verbs must be checked against usage rather than class membership
exceptions: verbs that admit both an object and a prepositional complement
a verb listed among the non-licensing group while being noted as able to take an object, which shows the class boundary is not clean
contrasts: object in the accusative versus prepositional complement in the genitive
base pattern versus causative augmented pattern of the same root

common_mistakes.pattern: placing a bare accusative noun after a verb that selects a preposition
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the verb does not license an object, so the noun has no assigner and must instead be governed by the preposition
common_mistakes.correction_principle: check the verb's selected frame first, and use its preposition with the genitive when it does not license an object

common_mistakes.pattern: treating the goal noun of a motion verb as its direct object
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the goal is reached through a preposition, so it is genitive and not accusative
common_mistakes.correction_principle: separate an argument that the verb assigns case to from one a preposition assigns case to

common_mistakes.pattern: assuming the base and causative patterns of one root have the same frame
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the augmentation changes argument structure, adding a causer and an affected participant
common_mistakes.correction_principle: re-evaluate the frame whenever the pattern changes, rather than inheriting it from the root

instructional_purpose: Sets out attributive modification (النعت والمنعوت) as agreement on four simultaneous axes, and shows that mismatching one of them either produces ungrammaticality or reanalyses the string as a predication rather than a phrase.
concepts_taught: attributive adjective and its head as a paired construction
agreement in case, gender, number and definiteness
case on the adjective as inherited from the head's syntactic role
feminine adjective formation by the feminine suffix
definiteness matching and the consequence of mismatch
non-human plural heads taking feminine singular modification
the phrase-versus-sentence contrast that hangs on the definiteness axis

linguistic_propositions.proposition: An attributive adjective agrees with its head on case, gender, number and definiteness simultaneously.
The head's syntactic role fixes its case, and the adjective copies that case rather than being assigned it independently.
A definite head with an indefinite adjective is not a phrase but a nominal sentence with the adjective as predicate.
Plural heads denoting non-humans take feminine singular modification.
The feminine of a descriptive adjective is normally formed by adding the feminine ending.
Number agreement requires singular with singular, dual with dual and plural with plural.

recognition_criteria: a noun immediately followed by a descriptive word carrying the same case exponent, the same definiteness marking and matching gender/number
a definite noun followed by an indefinite descriptive word, which signals predication rather than modification
a non-human plural head followed by a feminine singular descriptive word, which is modification and not a mismatch
the adjective's case exponent tracks whatever assigned case to the head, including after a preposition or as an object
procedures: fix the head noun's case from its role in the clause
read the head's gender, number and definiteness
build the adjective on the same four values
apply the non-human-plural override before setting gender and number
check that definiteness matches, since that axis decides phrase versus sentence
conditions: the override applies when the plural head denotes non-humans
definiteness matching is the axis that determines whether the string is a phrase at all
case agreement holds regardless of which governor assigned the case
exceptions: non-human plural heads do not take plural modification
a mismatch on the definiteness axis is not an error but a different construction
contrasts: definite head with definite adjective versus definite head with indefinite adjective
human plural agreement versus non-human plural agreement
the same adjective across the three cases as the head's role changes
masculine and feminine adjective shapes for the same head noun class

common_mistakes.pattern: modifying a non-human plural head with a plural adjective
common_mistakes.why_wrong: non-human plurals are modified as feminine singular, so a plural adjective violates the agreement rule for that head class
common_mistakes.correction_principle: classify the referent as human or non-human before setting the adjective's gender and number

common_mistakes.pattern: treating a definite noun followed by an indefinite adjective as a noun phrase

common_mistakes.correction_principle: read the definiteness axis first, then decide whether the sequence is modification or predication

common_mistakes.why_wrong: case agreement is one of the four required axes and the adjective must copy the head
common_mistakes.correction_principle: derive the head's case from its clause role and mirror the exponent on the adjective
